In general, Duluthians feel better prepared to address cold temperatures and winter storms than temperatures above 95% with high humidity. For outages over 5 days, 65.2% or residents would stay in their home without power during a winter storm/cold event versus 35.0% that would remain under extreme heat and humidity. Property Protection – Flooding was the final event- based standard created. It would require individuals to hold flood and/or renters’ insurance, perform rain-readiness assessments, and implement mitigation steps like sealing foundation cracks. Shared solutions for this standard included community mitigation projects using green infrastructure and maintaining a shared library of backup pumps and power sources to maintain power to sump pumps when necessary. Minimum resilience standards based upon individual vulnerabilities were prioritized for those dependent upon powered medical devices, temperature sensitive medication, and power-dependent mobility devices. These were considered the most sensitive minimum resilience standards because they address life-sustaining health and medical needs. The Powered Medical Devices standard mandates that all community members reliant on critical medical devices must have an emergency power plan to ensure their health and safety until power is restored or they can be relocated. Distributed actions necessitate partnering with medical teams and device suppliers to determine power alternatives (such as manual devices, home generators, or battery solutions) and ensuring device information is readily available to individuals and their care teams. Of the 21.7% of survey respondents that indicated that they, or someone in their household, used a powered home medical device, 54.1% stated that they do not have 18 an emergency power plan for their device(s) and 48.7% have no backup for charging during a power outage. Establishing resilience hubs that offer priority admission for individuals reliant on life-sustaining devices was suggested multiple times in interviews, however 57.0% of all residents said they were not at all likely or would not consider use of public emergency shelters/warming/cooling centers. Temperature Sensitive Medicine standard also requires establishing emergency plans and safe use or replacement protocols for medicine that may be compromised during an outage, with shelters/resilience hubs tasked with providing priority access to refrigeration. Research indicated a knowledge gap that could be filled through better communication between providers and residents. 19.2% of those surveyed indicated having someone in their household on temperature sensitive medicine. Of those, 34.4% indicated that they do not know what to do with their medicine during a power outage and 59.4% have not received, or did not remember ever receiving, information that would inform them on the continued viability/safety of their medicine if the temperature range has not been maintained. Finally, the Mobility standard dictates that individuals reliant on power-dependent mobility devices must have an emergency plan to ensure their ability to maintain safety or move to a safe location. Distributed actions involve documenting power instructions and possessing backup manual devices. Results indicated that shelter/resilience hubs should provide priority access to charging powered mobility devices and potentially maintaining a community library of manual mobility devices.
